title: But if it’s a man, what is a man going to prevent? Young men’s perspectives on pre-exposure prophylaxis use and persistence from a rural South African HIV prevention trial
content:
by Alison C. Castle, Lucky Nzimande, Thenjiwe Ncube, Bongani Nkosi, Emilia Mannstadt, Sweetness Dube, Christina Psaros, Jeremiah Chikovore, Maryam Shahmanesh, Mark J. Siedner

Young men who use alcohol in South Africa are at high risk for HIV yet remain underrepresented in prevention programs. This study explored social, cultural, and behavioral factors influencing PrEP initiation and persistence among young men who use alcohol in rural KwaZulu-Natal. We conducted 30 semi-structured individual interviews with men aged 18–34 years who reported alcohol use and had participated in a sexual health trial offering oral PrEP. Participants were purposively selected by PrEP engagement (declined, discontinued, or continued for ≥6 months). Interviews were conducted in isiZulu, transcribed verbatim, translated, and thematically analyzed using NVivo15. Participants had a median age of 27 years (IQR 24–32), were all sexually active, and had a median AUDIT-C score of 7 (IQR 5–9). Four themes shaped PrEP engagement. First, masculine norms and cultural identity fostered beliefs that “real men” should not need pills to stay healthy; traditional herbs and cleansing practices were often viewed as more trustworthy than biomedical prevention. Second, stigma and peer surveillance within social drinking networks heightened privacy concerns. PrEP’s resemblance to antiretroviral therapy generated fears of being labeled as living with HIV, reinforced through joking and gossip. Third, patterns of perceived HIV risk reinforced PrEP disengagement: some men acknowledged risk but avoided testing due to paralyzing fear of diagnosis, while others minimized risk based on partner trust or perceived self-control with sex. Finally, clear understanding of PrEP’s preventive purpose and alignment with personal values enabled some men to overcome social barriers, particularly when supported by youth-friendly mobile clinic delivery models. PrEP engagement among young men who use alcohol was driven primarily by sociocultural factors rather than access alone. Masculinity norms, stigma, and fear of HIV testing commonly sustained disengagement, while clear understanding of PrEP and delivery models supporting informed, self-directed decision-making facilitated use.
